clue.text: Johnny and Mark could be officially OK

parts.note: a johnny is British slang for a condom, also called a rubber
a stamp is a mark

explanation.surface: Someone mulls over whether a man called Johnny and his friend Mark would pass muster.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnny and Mark read as two men's names; both are ordinary nouns here, with johnny the British slang for a condom.
explanation.definitionFit: To rubber-stamp something is to approve it officially, often without scrutiny.

clue.text: Possibly put a cap on shivering critters?

indicators.note: shivering creatures are shaking, so the letters of critters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Cold, trembling little animals might need a woolly hat put on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' and the question mark warn that the image of capping animals is not literal; 'shivering' rearranges CRITTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: To put a cap on spending or numbers is to limit it, which is to restrict it.

clue.text: Totally support everyone in live format getting half cut

parts.note: to live is to be
the first half of FORMAT
everyone is all

explanation.surface: A plea for everyone to back a live show format that is being trimmed, with a hint of drunkenness in 'half cut'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half cut' is British slang for tipsy, but here it just chops a word in two; 'live format' reads as a TV term but splits across the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: being 'all for' a plan means backing it without reservation, which is what 'totally' adds.

clue.text: Listen with zeal to each plonk being brought over

parts.note: EA is the standard abbreviation for each, as on price tags

indicators.note: brought over means turned upside down, so in this down clue the word for plonk is read from the bottom up

parts.note: to plonk something is to put it down heavily

explanation.surface: Someone drinks in cheap wine for each person while eagerly listening; plonk is British slang for cheap wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Plonk looks like the cheap wine but is the verb 'put down'; 'being brought over' flips that verb upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat up words or music is to take them in eagerly, absorbing every bit with enthusiasm.

clue.text: More sentimental wimp must get support

parts.note: a sop is a weak, spineless person
a pier is a supporting pillar

explanation.surface: A wimp is told they need someone to lean on.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hides at the front, where 'more sentimental wimp' reads as one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Soppy means mawkishly sentimental; soppier is its comparative.

clue.text: A crew injecting heroin on a mountain top?

parts.note: as printed
a rowing eight is a crew
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A gang of addicts shooting up high on a peak.
explanation.walkthrough: H goes between A and EIGHT. AHEIGHT is an old adverb meaning on high, and the question mark flags a mountain top as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Aheight is an archaic word for aloft, so on a mountain top you are aheight.

clue.text: A bloated criminal beneath bow of police vessel

indicators.note: in a down clue, beneath places the rearranged letters under the opening letter of police
the bow is the front of a boat, so the bow of police is its opening letter

parts.note: its first letter is P

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked or bent, so the letters of A BLOATED are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A fat crook sits below the front of a police launch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' looks like a description of the bloated man but tells you to rearrange; 'bow of' is apt for a boat's front, and 'beneath' works because this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedal boat is a small craft propelled by pedalling, a kind of pleasure vessel on lakes.

clue.text: Welsh earl heading to major Shropshire town

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for earl in peerage lists

indicators.note: heading to takes just the front letter, the head, of the next word

parts.note: its first letter is M

explanation.surface: A Welsh nobleman sets off for an important town in Shropshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'major' reads as describing the town, but only its first letter is used. Shropshire is an English county on the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: Wem is a small market town in north Shropshire, England, so it is an example of a town there.

clue.text: Piece of seafood sparkles after being shelled

indicators.note: shelling removes the outer casing, so the word for sparkles loses its first and last letters

parts.note: twinkles means sparkles, shines with flickering light

explanation.surface: A morsel of shellfish glints once its shell is taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after being shelled' strips the outer T and S from TWINKLES.
explanation.definitionFit: A winkle is a small edible sea snail, a classic item of British seaside shellfish.

clue.text: After dumping soldiers, recollect one of many here?

indicators.note: dumping means throwing out

parts.note: to recollect is to remember
RE is the Royal Engineers

explanation.surface: Someone who has dumped their army mates tries to recall whether they were one of the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: REMEMBER minus RE leaves MEMBER. 'Here' points at the word itself: a member of 'many' is one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: any single person belonging to a large body, such as Parliament, is one of its many.

clue.text: A vertical passageway? Quiet at the back!

parts.note: sh is a call for quiet
aft means at the back of a ship

explanation.surface: A teacher asks what a vertical passageway is, then snaps at the chatterers in the back row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet at the back!' reads as a teacher's command; aft is the nautical word for the rear of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A mine or lift shaft is a vertical passage.

clue.text: My nude pose mostly excited Hoskins, for example

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all of the word pose, so its final letter goes

parts.note: taken as written, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone recalls their racy naked modelling session getting them worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts POSE to POS; 'excited' rearranges MY NUDE POS. Hoskins is this puzzle's setter, writing under an assumed name.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoskins is the setter's crossword alias, an assumed name used instead of their real one.

clue.text: A pilsner drunk by German back on the sauce?

indicators.note: drunk means intoxicated and reeling, so these letters are scrambled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A German downs a lager and is drinking heavily again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges A PILSNER to RELAPSIN, followed by G. 'The sauce' is slang for alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone falling back into an old habit, such as heavy drinking after sobriety, is relapsing.

clue.text: The French could quarantine sick in this city

indicators.note: to quarantine is to shut something away inside

parts.note: le is French for the
sick means ill

explanation.surface: French authorities consider isolating the ill in one of their cities.
explanation.walkthrough: The French article supplies the outside letters, and the French setting of the surface also fits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lille is a large city in northern France.

clue.text: One getting high from, and later coming down on, H?

definitions.text: One getting high from, and later coming down on
definitions.meaning: the surface reads a drug user's high and comedown; really something rising into the air and landing
not heroin but the big H painted on a helipad

explanation.surface: A drug user gets high on heroin and then suffers the comedown.
explanation.walkthrough: H looks like heroin slang, but it is the H painted on a helipad, where a helicopter takes off and lands.
explanation.definitionFit: A chopper is a helicopter, which rises from and descends onto a helipad marked H.

clue.text: Barking spaniel my boss subjected to discipline

indicators.note: barking is slang for mad, so the letters of spaniel go crazy into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the setter's boss is the crossword editor, ED

explanation.surface: A noisy dog belonging to the speaker's boss gets told off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' (British slang for crazy) rearranges SPANIEL to PENALIS, then ED, the editor who is the setter's boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone penalised has been punished or had a sanction imposed, as for breaking a rule.

clue.text: Implement gyration of booty

indicators.note: a gyration spins the word round

parts.note: booty is loot

explanation.surface: An instruction to twerk.
explanation.walkthrough: Booty and gyration suggest a dance move, but booty is plunder here.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a hammer or a spade is both a tool and an implement, a hand-held thing for doing work.

clue.text: Burning to get a hold of large queen for sure!

parts.note: burning means alight
L is the standard abbreviation for large
R is Regina, queen

explanation.surface: Someone is desperate to lay hands on a big queen, perhaps a drag star.
explanation.walkthrough: L and R go inside ALIGHT, after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'All right!' is an exclamation of agreement, like 'for sure!'.

clue.text: Incorrigible husband perhaps did some weeding topless

parts.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband
weeding is one kind of gardening, so GARDENED, minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A husband beyond reform does the weeding with his shirt off.
explanation.walkthrough: Topless paints a bare-chested gardener, but only takes the G off GARDENED; 'perhaps' marks weeding as one example of gardening.
explanation.definitionFit: A hardened criminal is set in his ways, incorrigible.

clue.text: After turning over, make love with boss

indicators.note: turning over flips the word

parts.note: bonk is British slang for having sex

explanation.surface: Someone rolls over after sex with their employer.
explanation.walkthrough: Boss looks like the employer, but it is the other sense: a round stud or knob.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is a round raised knob, as on a shield or ceiling.

clue.text: Rats on board tucked into cream for the most part

parts.note: the cream is the best; BEST without its last letter
a tray is a flat board for carrying things

explanation.surface: Rodents on a ship nibble at the dairy stores.
explanation.walkthrough: Rats reads as the animals but is the verb: to rat on someone is to betray them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rats on friends betrays them.

clue.text: One shielding joint quietly had knocked back a couple of lines

parts.note: p (piano) means quietly
had a meal means ate

indicators.note: knocked back means sent backwards

parts.note: A plus L and L, two lines

explanation.surface: A pot smoker quietly takes a drag on a joint, then snorts two lines of cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: Joint, knocked back and lines all suggest drugs and drink; joint is the knee, and only 'a couple of lines' is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: The patella, or kneecap, protects the front of the knee joint.

clue.text: That Bow lass after wine becomes a fool

parts.note: plonk is British slang for cheap wine
a Cockney from Bow would say 'er for her

explanation.surface: A girl from Bow makes an idiot of herself after drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is in the East End of London, and Cockneys drop the H, so 'that lass' there is 'ER. Plonker is British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: plonker is a mild insult for a fool, made famous by the sitcom Only Fools and Horses.

clue.text: One quickly kissing noble hugging man in pants?

parts.note: a peer is a nobleman
Calvin Klein, whose initials are on the waistband of underpants

explanation.surface: A lord in his underwear plants a hurried kiss on someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants are underpants in British English, and the man whose name is on them is Calvin Klein. Pecker also has a ruder sense that the surface nods at.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick kiss is a peck, so one who gives it is a pecker.

clue.text: Go up and start on cast during a broadcast

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: as printed
to broadcast is to send out
the first letter of cast

explanation.surface: Someone heads upstairs to get the actors going during a live show.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes inside SEND, and the leading A stays in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: climbing a staircase or a mountain is both going up and ascending it.

clue.text: One supporting a painter's current work?

definitions.meaning: the surface suggests a patron backing an artist; really something physically holding a thing up
not the latest project but the actual canvas being painted right now

explanation.surface: A patron backing an artist's latest project.
explanation.walkthrough: Supporting reads as sponsoring, but it is physical: the easel holds the canvas being worked on.
explanation.definitionFit: An easel is the stand that holds a painter's canvas while it is being painted.

clue.text: Tense trader's rear banker ruddy pinched on the sly

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of trader
a banker is something with banks, a river; the Ouse is an English river
ruddy means red

explanation.surface: A nervous dealer's backside is secretly groped by a red-faced banker.
explanation.walkthrough: Banker is a crossword name for a river, the thing with banks. To trouser money is British slang for pocketing it, often dishonestly.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouser cash is to pocket it, so trousered means pinched on the sly.

clue.text: Tender northern dons make some noise in bed?

parts.note: tender means sore
N is the standard abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: Amorous university lecturers from the north make a racket between the sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: Dons looks like academics, but it is the verb: to put on. The question mark hints the noise is not the one the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: snoring is one kind of noise a sleeper makes, and the question mark admits there are others.

clue.text: Quickly look over small defender in reserves

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the word for quickly look is read backwards

parts.note: to peek is to take a quick look
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
a back is a defending player in football or rugby

explanation.surface: A manager glances over a small defender among the substitutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns PEEK into KEEP; add S and BACK. 'Reserves' looks like the substitutes' bench but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep back something is to hold it in reserve, withholding it for later use.

clue.text: Men brought back horse for a music producer

parts.note: OR, other ranks, is the military abbreviation for ordinary soldiers, men

indicators.note: brought back means returned the other way, so the word for horse is read backwards

parts.note: a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: Soldiers return a horse in exchange for someone who makes music.
explanation.walkthrough: Men as 'other ranks' is a stock crossword convention; 'brought back' reverses the horse word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ is a keyboard instrument, something that produces music when played.

clue.text: Fisherman in Ohio breaking flipping bones

indicators.note: breaking into means splitting the reversed letters apart and sitting between them
flipping means turning over, so the abbreviation for bones is read backwards

parts.note: Bones, from sawbones, is slang for a doctor, abbreviated DR
O is an old postal abbreviation for Ohio

explanation.surface: An angler in Ohio has broken some bones while somersaulting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' turns DR into RD, and 'breaking' puts O between those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rod is an old word for an angler, the person wielding the fishing rod, by metonymy.

clue.text: Denser idiot must get bewildered and confused

indicators.note: bewildered letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the letters of DENSER IDIOT rearranged

explanation.surface: A particularly dim fool is bound to end up lost and muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: Bewildered and confused sit side by side as near-synonyms, but only the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who has lost their bearings is muddled, so confused and disoriented are interchangeable.
